questions.prompt: Which runtime foundation should own provider support?
questions.description: Grok already has native Rust Chat Completions, Responses, and Messages adapters. Pi and OMP are TypeScript/Bun references rather than drop-in Rust libraries.
questions.recommendedAnswer: Keep provider, auth, account, catalog, and protocol ownership native in Rust. Use Pi and OMP as source/test references; add an optional compatibility broker only if a specific provider cannot be implemented safely in Rust.

options.label: Native Rust provider plane
options.description: Preserves one runtime and existing actor/event boundaries; ports only proven provider behavior.

options.label: Rust core with broker escape hatch
options.description: Native by default, with a versioned optional broker for exceptional unsupported flows.

options.label: pi-ai broker as primary
options.description: Broad TypeScript provider reuse, but adds RPC, packaging, credential, cancellation, and version-skew ownership.

questions.prompt: Which provider families must be first-release commitments?
questions.description: Select all mandatory families. Other providers can follow through compatible configuration or later adapters.
questions.recommendedAnswer: Commit to subscription OAuth, core API-key providers, cloud identity, and local/gateway engines; treat OMP's long tail as a tracked parity program rather than blocking the first usable release.

options.label: Subscription OAuth
options.description: Grok/xAI, Anthropic subscription, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Google Gemini CLI-style flows.

options.label: Core API-key providers
options.description: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, xAI, OpenRouter, and compatible hosted endpoints.

options.label: Cloud identity providers
options.description: Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex, and Azure credential chains.

options.label: Local and gateway engines
options.description: Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, LiteLLM, and generic compatible discovery.

options.label: OMP long-tail parity
options.description: Make nearly every current OMP interactive provider a first-release blocker.

questions.prompt: What should the local credential-security boundary be?
questions.description: Multiple accounts, refresh leases, quota blocking, and session affinity need durable metadata. The question is where secret material itself belongs.
questions.recommendedAnswer: Store account metadata, routing state, leases, and blocks in SQLite; store refresh tokens and API keys in the operating-system credential vault when available, with a protected local fallback and explicit migration/export behavior.

options.label: OS vault plus SQLite
options.description: Best local secret boundary; SQLite retains stable account IDs and routing metadata.

options.label: Protected SQLite only
options.description: OMP-like simplicity with 0600 storage, but secrets remain application-readable database text.

options.label: Auth broker from day one
options.description: Central refresh-token custody and shared accounts, with much higher initial operational scope.

questions.prompt: How should model catalog authority work?
questions.description: The project should not hand-maintain model lists. models.dev is rich but mutable and incomplete for transport; authenticated provider discovery can be more authoritative for availability.
questions.recommendedAnswer: Ship a validated models.dev-derived snapshot, refresh metadata asynchronously into a last-known-good cache, and let authenticated provider discovery override availability and provider-specific limits. Support explicit offline mode.

options.label: Snapshot plus runtime overlays
options.description: Fast/offline startup with fresh metadata and provider-authoritative availability.

options.label: Snapshot plus provider discovery
options.description: No runtime models.dev dependency; catalog freshness arrives through releases and provider APIs.

options.label: Live catalog at runtime
options.description: Always fresh when online, but startup and model selection depend on an external mutable service.

questions.prompt: What must the first implementation milestone prove?
questions.description: The milestone should be independently useful and validate the architecture before broad provider fan-out.
questions.recommendedAnswer: Land the native provider/auth/account/catalog foundations and prove them vertically through Grok/xAI, Anthropic, OpenAI, and one local compatible engine, including login, account selection, streaming, tools, reasoning, persistence, refresh, failure handling, and TUI model selection.

options.label: Foundation plus vertical slices
options.description: Proves the boundaries across first-party, OAuth/API-key, and local-compatible routes before scaling out.

options.label: Broad provider parity first
options.description: Treat provider count as the first milestone, accepting more parallel adapter work before architecture hardening.

options.label: Login and picker UX first
options.description: Polish the current custom-model surface before replacing catalog/account internals.
